name: Stream processing engines
parent_research_topic: Beava's current market position — competitor archetypes and market segments beava is positioned in or against

competitive_landscape.incumbents: The stream-processing engine category in 2025-2026 is anchored by Apache Flink (24k+ GitHub stars, the de-facto enterprise stateful-streaming engine — Alibaba runs 40B events/day on it, plus Netflix, Uber, Stripe, LinkedIn, DoorDash, Lyft, BMW, Apple), Apache Spark Structured Streaming (now with Real-Time Mode GA — sub-300 ms p99 stateful, 5 ms minimum end-to-end — on Databricks Runtime 16.4+), Materialize (BSL 1.1, Postgres-compatible streaming materialized-view database, Community Edition capped at 24 GiB RAM / 48 GiB disk per install, $108M raised through Series C 2021, reported layoffs / 'uncertain transitional period' on Glassdoor in 2024-2025), RisingWave (Apache-2.0, Rust, ~8.8k GitHub stars, ~$46M raised, single-binary + distributed modes, Postgres-compatible, vector + MCP support added 2026), ksqlDB (Confluent — no formal EOL but feature-frozen since Confluent's 2023 Immerok acquisition pivoted them to Flink SQL on Confluent Cloud; ksqlDB still ships in Confluent Platform 8.2 but new Confluent investment is in Flink), Kafka Streams (the JVM-embedded option for Kafka-native teams). New-shape entrants gaining mindshare in 2025-2026: Arroyo (Rust, single binary, 5x sliding-window throughput vs Flink in published benchmarks), Bytewax (Python, Timely Dataflow under the hood), Pathway (Python + Rust), Fluvio (Rust + WASM), EventFlux (Rust, single-binary, 1M+ EPS at 50-100 MB RAM). The 2025-2026 trend is unmistakable: Flink-equivalent semantics in a single Rust binary with no JVM, no Kafka cluster prerequisite, no Zookeeper / KRaft / RocksDB tuning — exactly the architectural neighborhood beava lives in, though beava's scope is narrower (per-entity windowed aggregates, not general stream processing). Beava is NOT a stream-processing engine — it is a windowed-aggregation feature server, so the honest comparison is against the subset of Flink/Materialize/RisingWave use cases that build per-entity rolling counters for online serving.
competitive_landscape.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: For use case 5 (behavioral analytics / live product analytics): Flink + Kafka is the textbook DIY stack (DoorDash processes hundreds of billions of events/day on this combo, DoorDash's Riviera feature framework is a declarative Flink-based real-time feature engine); Spark Real-Time Mode is the Databricks-native answer (used for live personalization, ML feature computation, ad attribution per Databricks 2025 GA blog). Materialize and RisingWave both target the 'streaming materialized view powering same-session personalization' shape directly. For use case 13 (IoT telemetry rollups): Flink is the de-facto IIoT pipeline engine (cited in Confluent, Kai Waehner, Rivian+VW, Tesla Fleet Telemetry public references); RisingWave has published case studies of streaming-batch reconciliation for industrial IoT monitoring with HiveMQ MQTT brokers; Spark Structured Streaming is common where the buyer already owns Databricks; ksqlDB is occasionally seen but feature-frozen. For use case 14 (observability per-tenant rolling rates): Flink is rarely used directly — observability buyers reach for Prometheus + recording rules, Grafana Mimir (1B active series scale), VictoriaMetrics, or Cloudflare Workers Analytics Engine; the streaming-engine competitor here is the streaming-materialized-view shape (RisingWave / Materialize) being pitched as a 'recording rule replacement' for tenant × route cardinality. Funding/M&A status: Confluent (Flink's primary commercial vendor outside Ververica) is public (NASDAQ:CFLT); Materialize has not raised since the $60M 2021 Series C and shows public layoff signal; RisingWave has held at ~$46M since 2022; the Rust-single-binary entrants (Arroyo, Bytewax, Pathway, Fluvio) are mostly seed/Series A scale.
competitive_landscape.oss_license_posture: Mixed and increasingly a hard buyer filter in 2025-2026. Apache-2.0: Flink (Apache Software Foundation), RisingWave (the explicit Apache-2.0 challenger to Materialize, marketed on the license differential), Spark Structured Streaming (Apache, but Real-Time Mode is Databricks-runtime-exclusive in practice — proprietary gating), Kafka Streams (Apache), ksqlDB (Confluent Community License — source-available but not OSI-OSS, with restrictions on competing managed services). BSL: Materialize 1.1 with 4-year Apache-2.0 conversion plus an 'additional use grant' allowing non-DBaaS production use, and a Community Edition capped at 24 GiB RAM / 48 GiB disk. Proprietary / managed-only: Confluent Cloud Flink, AWS Managed Service for Apache Flink (MSF), Databricks Real-Time Mode runtime extensions. Beava's Apache-2.0 status is a real wedge against Materialize specifically (license-policy-blocked at any organization with a BSL ban) and a soft wedge against the managed-only options.
competitive_landscape.hyperscaler_bundling_threat: High. This is the dominant 2025-2026 distribution dynamic for the category. Confluent Cloud for Apache Flink is the most aggressive bundle (Kafka + Flink + Schema Registry + Connect in one SKU, AWS/Azure/GCP-resident, list-priced to migrate ksqlDB users to Flink). AWS Managed Service for Apache Flink (MSF) plus MSK is the AWS-native equivalent. Databricks Real-Time Mode lands Flink-equivalent sub-300 ms p99 latency inside the same Spark runtime customers already pay for — Databricks blog explicitly markets RTM as 'ultra-low latency streaming on Spark APIs without a second engine', which collapses the buyer's reason to bring in a separate streaming engine. Snowflake's Snowpipe Streaming + Dynamic Tables and Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence are the same play from adjacent hyperscalers. Net effect: a buyer in the streaming-engine market who already has a hyperscaler relationship rarely evaluates an independent engine in 2025-2026 unless the use case is specifically not fit (sub-ms p99, single-binary edge, tens-of-MB RAM, no JVM). That niche — which is exactly beava's positioning — is the only credible wedge against the hyperscaler bundle.
competitive_landscape.integration_surface: Stream-processing engines expect Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis, Redpanda, or AWS-IoT / Azure-IoT / MQTT as upstream producers, with CDC connectors (Debezium) for database sources. Flink ships the broadest connector library (hundreds of source/sink connectors via Flink CDC, FLIP-27 source API). RisingWave ships Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis, MQTT, MySQL/Postgres CDC, S3, Iceberg natively. Materialize ships Kafka and Postgres CDC primarily. Spark Real-Time Mode reads from Kafka and Delta Lake / Iceberg. Sinks are typically Kafka topics, JDBC databases, S3/Iceberg/Delta, ClickHouse, Pinot. Beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 + framed TCP+msgpack :8081 push surface is fundamentally different — it expects the producer to push events to beava (matching how SDK collectors like Segment, RudderStack, Snowplow, PostHog, Mixpanel, and HTTP-egress IoT brokers like AWS IoT Rules and Azure IoT Hub egress routes already work), not for beava to consume a Kafka topic. This is a fit for SDK-first behavioral analytics (use case 5) and AWS-IoT-Rules-style IoT egress (use case 13), and a friction for any buyer who has already standardized on Kafka and expects a streaming engine to consume from the bus (the entire DoorDash/Uber/Lyft/Rivian/Volkswagen archetype). Adding a Kafka consumer bridge is a few-hundred-line job but its absence is a real adoption blocker for the Kafka-first buyer; conversely, beava's HTTP-first ingest is friendlier than Flink/Spark for the not-yet-Kafka buyer.
competitive_landscape.scoring_engine_coupling: Stream engines couple to both rule engines (Drools, OPA, Flink CEP itself for in-engine pattern matching) and ML scorers (the engine pre-aggregates rolling features, an external scorer reads them at decision time). Materialize and RisingWave often serve query results directly to applications via Postgres protocol — they sit in the data path. Beava lives in the data path as a feature backend (read by external scorers and rules engines), never the decisioning path itself — matching the Flink-as-feature-pipeline-not-decision-engine pattern.

beava_position_lens.beava_credible_wedge: 1) Apache-2.0 with no open-core rug and no BSL gate — a hard differentiator against Materialize (BSL) and a soft differentiator against managed-only Spark RTM / Confluent Cloud Flink / AWS MSF. 2) Single binary, no JVM, no Kafka prerequisite, no Zookeeper / KRaft / RocksDB tuning — beava boots in milliseconds at tens of MB of RAM, where a baseline Flink job demands a JobManager + TaskManagers + state-backend + checkpoint sink. 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get for the serve side — Flink and Spark are pipeline engines that write to an external store for online serving; beava is the store, eliminating one hop. 4) ~60 pre-built aggregation primitives (count, sum, mean, var, std, n_unique, quantile via t-digest, HLL, CMS, exponential decay, recency, velocity, distance) expressed in a Python SDK — no Flink SQL, no Java DataStream API, no Spark Scala, no Materialize PostgreSQL DDL. 5) Push-on-event HTTP/TCP ingress matches the SDK-first behavioral-analytics shape (use case 5) and the AWS-IoT-Rules / Azure-IoT-Hub egress shape (use case 13) far better than Kafka-first engines. 6) The 'streaming materialized views converging with OLAP' trend (RisingWave + Materialize + Spark RTM all pitching MV-as-serving-store) validates the architectural seam beava sits in — except beava skips the SQL surface and ships pre-aggregated features directly, trading expressivity for sub-ms serve latency. The honest framing: beava is not a Flink competitor, it is the 'per-entity rolling-counter slice' of what teams build on top of Flink + Redis / Flink + Cassandra, collapsed into one binary.
beava_position_lens.beava_disqualifiers: 1) No general stream-processing — beava does NOT do windowed joins, CEP, complex event patterns, cross-stream enrichment, or arbitrary SQL transforms. The buyer who actually needs Flink's DataStream API or Flink CEP cannot replace Flink with beava. Honest scope: beava covers the count / mean / quantile / decay slice, not the 'stream-process my whole pipeline' job. 2) No Kafka consumer / no Kinesis consumer / no Pulsar consumer in v0 — every published Flink production reference (DoorDash, Uber, Lyft, Rivian+VW, Tesla, Stripe, Netflix) assumes Kafka is the source of truth; beava's HTTP/TCP-push model requires the buyer to add a bridge or wire their producer differently. 3) No exactly-once semantics — Flink's checkpointing + 2PC sinks, Spark's idempotent micro-batch + Delta, RisingWave's barrier-based checkpoints all guarantee exactly-once; beava is at-least-once at best. 4) No event-time processing in v0 — beava is processing-time-only and rejects `event_time` / `event_time_ms` fields explicitly (unknown_field_event_time_v0), which disqualifies any use case where late-arriving events must be windowed correctly (IoT telemetry with intermittent connectivity, mobile SDK buffered uploads, replay from a Kafka archive). Flink/Spark/Materialize/RisingWave all handle event-time + watermarks natively. 5) No TLS, no auth — disqualifying anywhere events cross trust boundaries (most production deployments). 6) No in-process sharding — a single beava node caps around 684k EPS / tens of GB hot state, where Flink/Spark/RisingWave routinely scale horizontally to millions of EPS. 7) No SQL surface — Materialize, RisingWave, Flink SQL, ksqlDB, Spark SQL all let analysts write CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW; beava only serves features declared in its Python SDK. 8) v0 events-only / no `kind: table` register, no joins, no sessions, no triggers — explicitly out of scope per locked invariants, but each is something a Flink user would have.
beava_position_lens.time_to_credible_offering: 6-12mo. To be a credible 'lightweight Flink alternative for the per-entity rolling-counter slice' the gating items are (a) a Kafka/Kinesis/MQTT consumer bridge so the buyer doesn't have to re-plumb their producers, (b) TLS + auth so it can cross trust boundaries, (c) event-time + watermarking so late-arriving events don't break IoT and CDC use cases, (d) some form of horizontal sharding or replication for the >684k EPS / >50 GB hot-state tenants, (e) at least an at-least-once-with-idempotency-key story matching MQTT QoS 1. None individually is a multi-quarter job, but together they are a 6-12 month roadmap before beava is credible to a buyer comparing it against Flink for a production behavioral-analytics or IoT-telemetry deployment.

evidence_and_verdict.validation_signals_today: No public beava users on stream-processing-engine-replacement workloads identified. [uncertain] The use-case-level deep-dives (5, 13, 14) explicitly flag 'no public users of beava on this use case' for behavioral analytics, IoT telemetry, and observability respectively. Repo evidence: ~60 aggregation primitives in python/beava/_agg.py covering the count / sum / mean / var / std / n_unique / quantile / HLL / CMS / exponential-decay / recency / velocity / distance surface that Flink / RisingWave / Materialize users hand-roll on top of their engines; demos exist for ecommerce and fraud-shaped flows but no purpose-built behavioral-analytics / IoT-telemetry / observability demo as of the current snapshot. Comparable adoption signals at incumbents: Flink production cited at Alibaba (40B events/day), DoorDash (hundreds of billions of events/day on Kafka+Flink), Uber, Lyft, Stripe, Netflix, Rivian+VW (>5,500 telemetry signals every 5 s per vehicle), Tesla (500 ms cadence), BMW, Apple, LinkedIn. RisingWave at 8,800+ GitHub stars with a published industrial-IoT-monitoring-with-HiveMQ-MQTT case study and partnership announcements (Systex, June 2025). Materialize visible layoff / 'uncertain transitional period' signal on Glassdoor in 2024-2025. Spark Real-Time Mode GA on Databricks Runtime 16.4+ in August 2025 with named customer adoption in financial services, e-commerce, media, ad-tech. The signal is that the category is mature, the buyer education already happened (sub-second streaming is the default expectation), and competing on raw streaming capability against any of these engines is not winnable in 2026; beava's only credible angle is the narrow 'per-entity feature serving without the engine' wedge.
evidence_and_verdict.verdict: Watch (do not directly compete on general stream-processing). Beava is structurally not a Flink/Spark/Materialize/RisingWave replacement — it covers the count/mean/quantile/decay slice of what teams build on top of those engines, collapsed into one binary. Position beava as the 'feature serving tier you put behind Flink (or instead of Flink + Redis) for per-entity rolling counters', not as a streaming-engine alternative. Monitor RisingWave specifically — it is the closest architectural cousin (Rust, Apache-2.0, single-binary-capable, materialized-view-as-serving-store) and is the engine most likely to expand into beava's territory by adding push-on-event ingress or a Postgres-protocol get-by-entity-key surface. Avoid framing battles where the buyer needs event-time + watermarks, exactly-once, or arbitrary SQL — beava loses those on day one.
